english: A person is driven by grief or toward a house of drinking and laughter. The comparison made is such that they choose some things and flee others in many ways, one of which is from those who choose. The wise man chooses virtue, piety, 'to please God', and strives for piety, even if he must die. But the many-sided man, the fool, does not choose these.

From the things chosen, virtue is preferred, because the wise choose it, not the coarse, not the exhausted, not the fool. And from the facts, again the comparison is taken, the beautiful thing said by those judging and comparing. The necessary thing is taken when we say that the soul is more excellent than the body, and it is more fitting to care for it rather than the body. From the matter, toward which the choice and comparison happen, the precious thing is taken, since the soul is more precious. He who is sparing and caring of it cares for the precious and the better according to truth.

And there is also when the preference happens from the things accompanying. Thus it is not necessary to prefer living simply over dying. For even if someone prefers living over the one about to die through clamor or the justice of a judge or something else pursuing Christianity and the truth, it is for a little while. For if he does not die by the murderer, sometimes a disease having seized him interrupts life; it has difference only in time, that he who is immediately subject to the wrath of a judge dies, but to be destroyed by disease, life's end is uncertain, when. However, this is not for an infinity, but in more time he may remain. And thus the judgment happens from the singularity or the speed of the matter.

It is good to hear the rebuke of a wise man rather than the songs of fools. It seems to many that the rebuke from the wise should be avoided, especially when they are lovers of sin. For he having the desire to enjoy and to sin avoids the one forbidding these things. He who has no opinion at all rejoices in flatteries; he wants rather to hear the songs of flattery than the words of rebuke. For it is the part of a wise man to love the one rebuking. For it is said in Proverbs: but the impious and the evil man hates the one rebuking. For he says: 'He who rebukes the impious will be blamed and himself.' For he blames himself, the one [rebuking] the impious...

For the impious man is to be rejected and forbidden. And just as a physician who subjects those unable to be cured by cutting or cautery to such things is not a physician, but an ignorant physician, so he who reproves the incorrigible reproaches himself more, for he provokes them to speak against him.

And they show that one having such a fault does not know whom to reprove and whom not to. Such is the rebuke of the wise over the laughter of fools. Flatterers sing in a certain way; even if they speak moral words, they wish more to please than to benefit those who hear. Laughter is a word that stirs up pleasure, but rebuke, being corrective and persuading one to cease former works, demonstrates them, making it clear that they are things to be avoided and forbidden.

Is it the wise man who rebukes or the one being rebuked? It is the rebuke of the wise, not that which he himself undergoes, but that which he imposes on others. If you wish to take it as 'the rebuke of the wise' being that which he himself undergoes, that is a violent interpretation, yet he says this: the wise man receiving rebuke corrects himself and casts away those things for which the rebuke happened to him, and this is good for him. But he does not mean this, but rather that which he brings to those worthy of rebuke, so that the saying might be similar to this: 'He who brings wisdom from his lips strikes a heartless man with a rod.'

Just as the sound of thorns under a cauldron is so, such is the laughter of fools. And this too is vanity. For the thorns, when they are burned under a cauldron, produce a great noise. And so the laughter of fools is such, until they produce noises; it is not for the sake of refreshing the soul. If the soul does not laugh, it has not yet reached the point of rebuking. Often in the writings, the cauldron signifies punishment. 'For a east wind shall burn from the face of the countenance upon those inhabiting the land' (Ezekiel 20:45), when the people mocked the prophet, they laughed. Fools do not laugh until they have made a noise and sounds; they are more like jesters. And just as the thorns themselves, being burned under the cauldron, emit a noise, so their laughter is from a scorched, evil soul.

english: Bringing forward those [things]. Furthermore, the upward leading: 'It is good to hear a rebuke from the wise.' The divine word of the Scriptures is wise, and each one of those guarding it is wise according to God, is God-wise. When therefore one such rebukes, is the effort good or not? And he rebukes well. But many rebuke even regarding not allowing someone to be a buffoon, for the sake of not dancing and doing such things. But the wise man brings forward a check against sin. And the rebuke, being such a thing of the wise, being improving, even if the one being improved is not improved, it is good beyond the folly of the foolish, the punishment of the word and not rebuking. And even if a man is harmed through the folly of the foolish, it is not only a woman or a child.

The worldly cares are indeed thorns, the shameful desires, the unrestrained pleasures. This he says: that such things, which those playing the buffoon think they do with pleasure, are thorns, bringing and coming under punishment. And this is vanity. For they will gain nothing from laughter; as you would say to one living badly: 'It is in vain for you.' For slander carries away the wise and destroys the good disposition of his heart. The 'carries away' is thus: often someone accuses the wise man badly and finds many following him. And if he was not entirely well-disposed and perfect, at times he also is shaken.

Susanna, her wise soul not being carried away, was slandered regarding adultery. And the slander was not being said against one or two false accusers; those ruling the people and judges of such accusations were the accusers. All the people paid attention to them as judges and as those ruling the people. And almost no one was a forger of the slander. When therefore, being God-wise, she perceived that in vain the things of the accusation were for her—for she would not find the one listening—she fled to God and with the spoken word she was silent, but with the mind she cried out: 'O God, the Eternal One, the Knower of hidden things, who knows all things before their being, you know that they testify falsely against me.' Slander did not carry her away, nor did it establish her in misery, but it confirmed her in sobriety. And Joseph likewise. And in the time especially of the persecutions, many...

They were flattered and not driven about. Therefore, the wise one here does not speak of the perfect one, but of the one having the beginning, the new one. Thus we have also understood: 'rebuke the wise, and he will love you'. The perfect wise man is not subject to any rebukes. For when it says, 'the wise will not depart from the mouth of the Most High' (Psalm 115:13), it speaks of the perfect ones here.

Many indeed sacrificed without even having a choice, 'the loss of the straightness of their heart'. For it is possible for toil to drive out a heavy intention not entirely all-powerful. A good end of words concerning his beginning, a good long-suffering concerning a high spirit. The end of the words rather has already something good concerning the beginning of the words.

The one beginning the word, in order that you may take the word here as active, the real one, implicitly has it, if he completes the word, if he acts according to the word. english: He teaches, and he rebukes in a similar way. He does not forbid by one rebuke or a second, but he also approaches health in another way. This long-suffering one is therefore better than the proud and the 'high in spirit'. Indeed, some say that if he speaks more slowly, it is a lesson, saying: 'Ah, a cleansing, go away, you are able to do nothing.' But what of the lifting up? The lifting up is that itself.

Because you desire this: the one believing in the Savior from among the Gentiles is long-suffering, but the people from the circumcision who say, 'We have no king but Caesar' [sic] and 'We are disciples of Moses' are high in spirit. Regarding this one who is high in spirit from the Hebrew people, the one from the Gentiles who became long-suffering because he has known the things concerning him—that 'having no hope and being without God in the world' (1 Thess 4:17; Eph 2:12)—is a precursor there. Do not hasten in a spirit of anger, for anger rests in the foolishness of a mind in a rage.

demonstrating. This one, then, does all things in the soul; but the one having ascended above this and doing with divine reasoning or sometimes with mere reasoning, this one does all things in the spirit.

This, then, I call knowledge, not being knowledge in the strict sense, but that which appears to those using it to be becoming bad. For a fool's passion rests in the heart. The one who is not a fool, but wise and attentive to prudence, even if something is ever seen or heard or moves the passion, it remains only until a passion occurs.

For the heart signifies the ruling principle in many of the divine lessons, as if it says: 'Their folly is in the land of Egypt in their heart' (Ps 106:27). So also it is said in other places that 'all things come into the heart of the unjust' (Prov 14:13). What he says is this: that he touches evils, and against his own ruling principle he brings harm and plague.

Again, if the holy man says: 'My prayer shall turn back into my heart,' the diligent man asks for that, sending a prayer to God, which is both beneficial for him to receive and proper for God to give. And his prayer turns back into his heart, bringing what he asked for. For he asks for nothing more than bodily strength or wealth, but for that which improves the mind.

If, therefore, it happens that what he asks for—since the things given do not remain outside of him, but in his disposition and in the ruling principle—his prayer turns back into his heart. Do not say: 'What happened that the former days were better than these?' (Phil 3:13). 'Better than these' is not merely said, but also reasoned: he who is beginning virtue and 'the illumination of the knowledge of truth' and being shone upon by the 'sun of righteousness' (Mal 4:2) always receives by the light; and just as the diligent man 'stretches toward the prize of the higher calling' (Phil 3:14).

The things being given are left behind, forgetting those from whom they have come, so that he no longer turns back and returns; 'stretching forward to those that are before' (Phil 3:14), he is made distant, he who began to be enlightened by the 'sun of righteousness' (Mal 4:2) and always receives by the light, as if to say that 'the first days were better than these' (Phil 3:13). And we say this somewhat poorly, but perhaps...

english: Speaking truthfully, we somewhat accuse ourselves that before this we were explaining well and we were approaching ourselves; we feared God. May it not be such a thing, he says, since the days to come are to be enlightened. But what of the one not knowing? He says this to himself, wondering, 'Why has this happened to me, that previously the days were good?' (Ps 90:16) because he did not inquire about this in wisdom. The inquiry was in wisdom: 'Why, that I have received this?' I have become better than myself; they received something greater instead of something lesser. This, therefore, is praise, being the same as 'I press on toward the goal for the prize of the upward call' (Phil 3:14), in greater days toward the promises, 'that your latter end may be a good land, and you shall be long of life on the earth' (Gen 28:14).

These days must be interpreted thus: 'This is your life and this is the length of your days: to love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your strength, and with all your soul' (Deut 6:5). This is the life of the ages, the length. He says this to the one being introduced here. Good wisdom with inheritance and abundance for those who look upon the sun. He says this: if this has become something improving the soul, approaching being in wisdom, it is good, if it possesses the inheritance. And I say: 'No one, he says, says Lord Jesus except in the Holy Spirit' (1 Cor 12:3), even though many call him Lord, but not truly, not in truth. For he says to them: 'Why do you call me Lord, Lord, and do not do what I say? Not everyone who says to me, Lord, Lord, will enter the kingdom of heaven, but he who does the will of my Father who is in heaven' (Matt 7:21). This, therefore, is the one truly saying Lord Jesus through the participation of the Holy Spirit. The one having been persuaded of wisdom according to the Holy Spirit makes [the wisdom of] Jesus. And this one truly says Lord Jesus. Just as 'no one says Lord Jesus except in the Holy Spirit,' so no one is good in wisdom not having its inheritance.

an inheritance, which he receives as he happens to come to it. For they are wise in appearance only until they speak, but not until they act. The wisdom that follows inheritance is not that which is being made, and it carries the divine promise of becoming possessed by the wise. And there is abundance for those contemplating the sun.

english: That the Lord has tested them. And again: 'silver given with deceit is to be regarded as an earthenware vessel.' If this presents a clever deceit, it is not like one having been 'cleansed sevenfold' or being regarded as such, not being established by itself, like one having the word of one who has been refined. For those who present a word that is earthly and have an earthly nature do not speak concerning wisdom. First, they have received an earthly nature.

For human wisdom is in a shadow and upon the earth. He says that its shadow is in wisdom, as the wisdom of silver, in which the wisdom is in its own shadow. If, therefore, he praises the being of wisdom, and its shadow is the best. What then is 'in the shadow of wisdom'? He who is speaking while being in the shadow of the Gospel is in the original Gospel, or he who is in the shadow of the Law. And the abundance of knowledge of wisdom will vivify the one who is from it. And this is good, to always enjoy in the progress of the contemplation of wisdom. 'He will vivify the one who is from it.' For this reason it is to be preferred and is good, because it makes the one participating in it alive—'the one who is from it,' he says, the one who is wise according to it—for the wisdom of life is not to be set aside. It never brings death to the soul.

Behold the works of God: for who will be able to turn away whom God turns? Many also among the Greeks have opposed those saying that the cosmos consists of things from themselves, such as Epicurus, and according to some, Democritus. For they think that this cosmos did not come from God, because they do not posit providence. Since every necessity is that the one being provided for should provide for his own works, and God is the one providing, He provides for the cosmos which He Himself made. Give the rest: that which He Himself constructed, this also He protects by providence, so that it may stand. Some therefore argue: 'If the cosmos was made best, what is the use of the basilisk existing? If the usefulness of being is entirely given, it is necessary for the basilisk and the others, such as the rhinoceros, to exist.' And it is more pleasing to the Epicurean to make mockery than praise. Because of these things, he generally rejects providence. But those who oppose the...

They believe this godless dogma. Who would say to the world that a part of the world needs straightening? How else could it have happened? How could it have been driven? How could a world be without parts? If these things, what are the parts? For neither are they shown to be passing by or in excess, if the world is able to consist out of them.

But we say that it is possible to persuade by a probable demonstration, both the cause and that the wild things were created for uses. And these things contribute to hunting. By a first common and right reason, it is possible to say that all things are for humans. Many of these things contribute to the help of them and [gap] receiving [gap] and intending [gap] receiving [gap]. From this, it is possible for a generation to be made manifest according to which they came to be, so that we might use only these, so that we might not torture any remaining or other higher discourse, because for the sake of humans even these things have come to be.

Therefore God knows the causes of the things having happened, and He knows why He hid them. According to all this He says only: 'Do not say: For what purpose is this? Or for what purpose is this? For all things shall be sought in their time' (Eccl 3:10-11). And: 'Do not say: For what purpose is this? Or for what purpose is this? For all things were created for their use' (Eccl 1:28).

Behold the works of God. Understand the works of God—for this 'behold' says it—understand also their existence and the reason according to which they are, and, if it is what it is, and the cause. 'For who will be able to arrange [the world]?' Many things contribute to perfect knowledge, and it is not possible for all things to exist for all people; for example, to say, I say, to be God or to be a world. It is sufficient for me regarding the 'that it is' to know only, and what the name placed against it means. But the 'how' is not for everyone to know, but not even for the one knowing everything is it possible to say the 'how'. It is possible [to know] by which word and knowledge. For indeed the [gap] observing [gap] and [gap] the one knowing [gap] through what it is, and that it is, and how it is. And in these, not everyone knowing that it is, knows also how it is and why. 'Behold' therefore 'the works of God', understand them, know what each of them is and that it is.

ε̣ἰ τὸ σῶμα σημειοῦται. κα̣ὶ ὃ λ̣ε´̣γει, ποιεῖ αὐτὸ ἀθεράπευτον, ἀνίατον ἀποδείκνυσιν. οὐ πάντως οὖν τὸ ποι̣ῆσαι τὸ ἐνεργῆσα̣ι δηλοῖ, ἀλλ' ἐν̣ίοτε τὸ ἀποδεῖξαι. ἔχεις γοῦν καὶ ἐν τῷ εὐαγγελίῳ ὑπὸ τῶν σεαυτὸν θεὸν ε̣ἶναι". οὕτω̣ς̣ α᾿̣κ̣ου στέον καὶ τοῦ "ἴσον ἑαυτὸν π̣οιῶν τῷ θεῷ", ἐπεὶ "πατέρα ἴδιον λέ γει τὸν θεόν". ἴσ̣α δε´̣ ἐστιν τὰ γεννη´̣μα̣τα τ̣ῷ γεννήσαντι̣ καὶ ἐκ τοῦ κατ' ἀλήθ̣ειαν λε´̣γ̣ε̣ιν τοῦτον̣ πατέρα ἔχειν ἴδιον̣ σεαυτὸν ἀπ̣ο δεικνύεις θεόν. ὁμοίως λημπτέον, ὅταν̣ λέγῃ· "ο῾̣ θ̣ε̣ο`̣ς̣ διαστρέφει". διαστρέφει γὰρ μ̣ὴ οὕτως ἐν̣εργῶν, ἀλλὰ ἀπο̣δείκνυσιν 23 αὐτὸν τοιοῦτον, ὡς "παραδίδω σίν̣ τινα εἰς ἀδόκι̣μον νοῦν", οὐκ αὐτ̣ὸς ἐνεργῶν. τὸ παραδοθῆναι αὐτοὺς ἐν τ̣ῷ ἀδοκίμῳ ὄντα̣ς̣ ἀποδείκνυσιν κ̣αὶ α̣ὐτο̣υ`̣ς παρ' ἑαυτοὺς τοιού τους γεγε̣νημένους. ὅταν οὖν ὁ θεὸς διαστρέφειν λέγηταί τινα, ἀπο δείκνυσιν διεστραμμένον τ̣ο´̣τε̣. ὃν ο῾̣ θεὸς οὖν α᾿̣ποδοκίμασεν κ̣αι`̣ ἀπ̣έδειξεν διαστραφέντα, "τι´̣ς δ̣υ´̣ν̣α̣ται ἐπικοσμῆσαι;" "τοὺς δὲ ἐκκλίνοντας", φησίν, "εἰς τὰς στραγγαλιὰς ἀπάξει κύριος μετὰ τῶν ἐρ γαζομένων τὴν ἀνομίαν". μὴ γὰρ αὐτὸς αὐτοὺς μὴ βουλομένους ἀπάγει μετὰ τῶν τὴν ἀνομίαν ἐργαζομένων, ἀλλ' ἐκκλίνοντας π̣ροαιρέσει τῇ αὐτῶν ἀπέ δειξεν αὐτοὺς "ἐν τῇ ἡμέρᾳ τῆς ἀγαθοσύνης". ἀγαθοσύνης ἡμέρα ἐστίν, ὅταν ἀρετὴ προσῇ. ζωῆς δὲ αὕτη περιποιητική ἐστιν. οὕτω οὖν ἔχε τὸ ζῆν ὡς ἀγαθός, ὡς ζωῆς μετέχων· μακαρίζῃ ἐν μακαρίοις. ἴσθι τὴν ζῳοποιητικὴν ἔχων διάθεσιν. ζῶν ἔσο ἐν αὐτῇ. ἐπερ· "ἐν ἡμέρᾳ ἀγαθοσύνης"; τὴν κατάστασιν τοῦ ἔχοντος. πολλάκις γὰρ καὶ αἱ καταστάσεις σημαίνον ται ὀνόματι καιρῶν καὶ χρόνων. ἐν ἡμέρᾳ κακίας. 213 ὡς ἔστιν ἀπὸ τῆς "ἡμέρας τῆς ἀγαθοσύνης" ὡς ἐν ἀγαθῷ, οὕτως ἐν ἡμε´̣ρᾳ τῆς κακίας ἐστὶν ζῆν φαύλως. ἀλλ' ἐσιώπησεν τὸ φαυ´̣λως, ἵνα μὴ λίαν ἀναγκαστικὸς ᾖν ὁ λόγος. σύνφωνον τοῦτο ἐκείνῳ ἐστίν, ὡς ἀπο`̣ τ̣η῀̣ς φ̣ρονήσεως τὸ φρονεῖν καὶ ἀπὸ τῆς ἀφροσύνης τὸ ἀφραίνειν ἀναλογίαν, οὐ τὴν ὁμοιότητα ἔχουσιν. συμφωνεῖ γοῦν τοῦτο ἐκείνῳ κατὰ ἀναλογίαν, οὐ κατὰ ποιότητα ἢ ποσότητα οὐδὲ τῶν
english: And what is the name applied to this, and how they presented it, and why? For you will not have sufficient knowledge of the works of God if you stumble against them without agreeing. Indeed, study the works of God; what caused stumbling to others will give to you the knowledge of both the Maker and of the things made.

For who will be able to order the world? I remembered that they call it 'the cosmos' [the ordered thing]. And he who blames this is considered to be accepting it; according to this it is possible to say: 'Whom do you call parts of the world?' For they themselves are the cosmos. [It is] so that the world may not have accusations; especially these things are drawn toward providence. For not only are the creatures the works of God, but also those according to His judgment in providence. We say that now it appears to the Creator of the world, who is being provided for, to order it through [death], [he] dies, and again he died. And he blames much of this. We say to him: 'How should it come to pass? Order [re-order] that which you think is disordered.' Therefore, no one has the power to say this. And indeed, it is for everyone to re-construct in this way, not saying the constructions. But reconstruction is after a construction, even if the man, having become through the word, does not call the construction the re-ordering. But nature is thus: whomsoever God turns away.

This is set down in the Levitical law concerning lepers. And this is the beginning of the law: if ever anyone receives a sensation of his body having become leprous, he shall approach the priest, and from the sign that one [the priest] would demonstrate, he would show him to be either a leper or not truly a leper, but a suspicion. And he says that the priest, having examined and finding that it is leprosy, 'shall defile him,' not that he performs the 'defiling' himself, but because he demonstrated him to be such a thing. But if he does not fall into it, he shall set him apart for a certain number of days. And after those, he shall be examined; if he remains healthy, the priest shall defile him. And a physician, indeed, observes a certain disease if the body is marked. And what he says, he does [it] as an unceasing [remedy], demonstrating it as incurable. So, not always does the act of doing signify the actual performing, but sometimes...

To demonstrate. You also have in the Gospel what is said by the Jews, that 'being a man, you make yourself God' (John 10:34). For they do not say: 'Being a man, you are preparing yourself to be God', but rather 'From those things which you announce and promise to do, you demonstrate yourself to be God'. Thus, hearing also [the phrase] 'making himself equal to God', since 'he calls God his own father'. The offspring are equal to the one who begot, and by saying this one is father according to truth, you demonstrate that you have a father of your own as God.

Similarly, it should be taken when it says: 'God turns away' (2 Thess 2:11). For He does not reject by acting [in that way], but demonstrates him to be such a person, as 'handing someone over to an unapproved mind', not by acting [Himself]. The handing them over to the unapproved demonstrates [their state] and that they have become such people by themselves. Therefore, when it is said that God turns away someone, He demonstrates him to be having been turned away.

Whom then God has rejected and demonstrated to be turned away, 'who is able to adorn them?'; 'but those turning away', He says, 'the Lord will lead away with the workers of lawlessness to the chains' (2 Thess 2:12). For not He himself leads them away against their will with those working lawlessness, but by their turning away of will, He demonstrated them to be such people.

Live in goodness in a day of goodness, and in a day of evil, behold, and this is in agreement with that. 'In the day of goodness'. A day of goodness is when virtue is present. And this of life is life-giving. Thus, to live as good is to live as a partaker of life; he is blessed among the blessed. Be, having the life-giving disposition. You shall live in it.

Regarding: 'in the day of goodness'? The state of the one having [it]. For often also the states signify the name of seasons and times. In a day of evil. Just as it is from the 'day of goodness' to live in the good, so in a day of evil it is to live poorly. But the 'poorly' was silenced, so that the word might not be too much of a necessity. This is in agreement with that, just as to think from prudence and to act from folly is an analogy, they do not have similarity. source_text: παρεπομένων. ἐποίησεν ο῾̣ θεὸς περὶ λαλίας, ἵνα μὴ εὕρῃ ἄνθρωπος ὀπί σω αὐτου῀̣ μηδέν. τὰ πάντα εἶδον ἐν ἡμέραις ματαιότη τός μου. ἐποίησεν ὁ θεὸς τοιοῦτον λόγον ἐν τοῖς οὖσιν, ἵνα ὁ ἄνθρωπος μὴ εὕ ρῃ μηδὲν τῶν μετ' αὐτὸν ἐσομένων. ὧδε π̣ρόγνωσιν ἀναιρεῖ ἀνθρωπίνην· οὐκ εὑρίσκε̣ι ὁ ἄνθρωπος οὐδὲν τῶν διαδεξομένων αὐτόν. πε̣ρ̣ι`̣ τ̣ῶν ἀν θρωπίνων δὲ λέγει. ὅτι γὰρ οἶδεν ὁ σπουδαῖος, ὅτι διαδέξεται αὐτὸν κατάστασις μακαρία, παντί που σαφές. εἰ μή, ἐὰν ἡ τοῦ ἀνθρώπου προσηγορία παρακειμένη ἄλλην ὑποβάλῃ διά νοιαν, ἄνθρωπον δὲ μ̣ὴ τὸ θνητὸν λογικὸν ζῷο̣ν λέγῃ, ἀλλὰ τὸν "κατὰ σάρκα" καὶ ἡδονὰς "περιπατοῦντα", ὁ τοιοῦτος ἄνθρωπος, ᾗ τοιοῦτός ἐστιν, οὐδὲν διαγνώσεται τῶν διαδεξομένων̣ αὐτόν, ἅτε δ̣ὴ αἰσθήσει μόνῃ ζῶν. ἡ γα`̣ρ αἴσθησις τὰ παρόντα καταγ̣ιγνώσκει. ἐπ̣εὶ ὁ τοιοῦτος ὅλος τῆς αἰσθήσεώς ἐστιν, "κατὰ σάρκα" καὶ ἡδονὰς καὶ τὰς ἄλλας κακίας περιπατῶν, τὰ "ὀπίσω", τὰ διαδεξόμενα, οὐκ οἶδεν. νοῦ γὰρ ἔστιν τοῦτο εἰδέναι. ἐν ταῖς ἡμέραις μου οὖν τῆς ματαιότητος τὰ πάντα εἶδον. ἡμέρας δὲ ματαιότητος λέγει τὰς ἡμέρας τῆς ζωῆς ταύτης, ἐφ' ᾗ οὐ δεῖ αὐτὸν ἐλπίζειν. ἐλεεινοὺς γὰρ κατασκευάζει τοὺς προσδοκοῦντας. ἔστιν δίκαιος ἀπολλύμενος ἐν δικαίῳ αὐτοῦ· καὶ ἔστιν ἀσεβὴς μένων ἐν κακίᾳ αὐτοῦ. ἔστιν ἁπλῶς δίκαιον καὶ ἔστιν τινὸς δίκαιον. ὅταν οὖν ὁ θεῖος προσ τάττῃ λόγος "δικαίως τὸ δίκαιον διώκειν", οὐχ ἑκάστῳ λέγει ὅτι "δι καίως τὸ δίκαιόν σου δίωκε", ἀλλὰ τὸ ἁπλῶς καὶ κυρίως δίκαιον. ἐπειδὴ δὲ πᾶς ἄνθρωπος φαίνεται ἑαυτῷ δίκαιος καὶ "εἰσὶν δοκοῦσαι ἀνθρώπῳ ὀρθαὶ ὁδοὶ εἶναι, τὰ τελευταῖα βλέποντα εἰς πυθμένα ᾅδου", οὐκ ἐν 214 ἐκείνῳ τῷ δικαίῳ δεῖ ἐνμένειν. ἀπόλλυσιν γὰρ τοῦτον τὸν ἔχοντα, φθεί ρει τὸν ἔχοντα. ἔστιν οὖν δίκαιος ἀπολλύμενος ἐν δικαίῳ ἑαυτοῦ. οἱ δ̣ὲ κατ' α᾿̣λήθειαν δίκαιοι, περὶ ὧν πολλὰ γέγραπται, οἷον· "δίκαιοι ποιήσουσιν ἐν πλούτῳ ἔτη πολλά", οὗτοι οὐκ ἐν δικαίῳ ἑαυτῶν ἐνμένου σιν, οὐ θαρροῦσιν τῷ ἑαυτῶν̣ δικ̣αίῳ. διὸ οὐκ ἀπόλλυται ἐν τῇ δικαι οσύνῃ, ὡς λέγει ὁ ὑμνῳδός· "ἐν τῇ δικαιοσύνῃ σου ζήσομαι". Παῦλος γοῦν, μέγας ἄνθρωπος ὑπάρχων καὶ ἐν Χριστῷ τυγχάνων, ᾧ και`̣ η῾̣ ἀποκάλυ ψις τη῀̣ς̣ ἀληθείας γέγονεν, λέγει· "οὐδὲν ἐμαυτῷ συνοῖδα, ἀλλ' οὐκ ἐν τούτ̣ῳ δεδικαίωμαι". ἐνχωρεῖ γάρ με μὴ τὸ ἀληθῶς english: Passing over [these things]. God made [the world] in such a way regarding speech, so that no man might find anything behind Him. 'All things I saw in the days of vanity' (Eccl 1:2). God made such a word in the things that exist, so that man might find nothing of those that are to follow him.

Here he invalidates human foreknowledge; man finds nothing of those who will receive him. And concerning human things he says: for the diligent man knows that he will receive a blessed state, which is clear everywhere. If not—if the human designation, being present, submits another through thought, and if he calls man not the mortal rational animal, but the one 'walking according to the flesh' and pleasures—such a man, being such, will not be recognized by those who are to follow, as long as he lives by sensation alone. For sensation recognizes only the present things. Since such a man is entirely of sensation, walking 'according to the flesh' and pleasures and other evils, he does not know the 'behind', the things that are to follow. For it is the intellect to know this.

In the days of my vanity, therefore, I saw all things. And 'the days of vanity' (Eccl 1:2) he means the days of this life, upon which he must not hope. For he prepares those who expect [to be] miserable. There is a righteous man perishing in his own righteousness; and there is an ungodly man remaining in his own wickedness. There is simply righteous, and there is someone's righteous. When therefore the Divine, in that word, says 'to pursue the righteous thing justly', he does not say to each one, 'pursue your own righteous thing justly', but the simply and principally righteous. Since every man seems righteous to himself and 'the last ways seem to be right to man, looking into the pits of Hades', one must not remain in that [subjective] righteousness. For he who has this destroys him, and he withholds from the one who has it. There is therefore a righteous man perishing in his own righteousness. But those who are righteous according to truth, about whom much has been written, such as: 'the righteous shall do in wealth many years' (Ps 112:9), these do not remain in their own righteousness; they do not trust in their own righteousness. Therefore he does not perish in righteousness, as the hymnodist says: 'in your righteousness I shall live' (Ps 25:10). Paul, then, being a great man and finding himself in Christ, to whom was the revelation of yours...

It has become a matter of truth, he says: 'I do not know anything to myself, but not in this have I been justified.' For it enters into me, that I do not truly possess righteousness, and not because of this—that I have known nothing to myself of those things that harm—[am I] justified. And again the holy David says: 'If I saw iniquity in my heart, let not the Lord hear' (Psalm 138:23). A sign of having or not having iniquity is whether one is heard by God or not heard.

And it is possible also to take this in another way according to a second explanation: it is to cause someone to perish from his own righteousness; someone thinking himself righteous in his own righteousness, if... he knows that it is not the truth and the Lord of righteousness, he pulls himself away from this and perishes from his own righteousness. And this destruction does not corrupt. For just as we say of one departing from virtue that he has perished by virtue, so we say of one having changed from the presumption he formerly held, that he has perished from that presumption.

And there is an impious man remaining in his own wickedness, living in wickedness not recognizing his own wickedness, even though he was previously recognized as a righteous man before he was justifying himself. Is it then the same mind? That [mind], even though being in righteousness, yet being less than the truly righteous, perishes from it, so that he may have the truly righteous. For example, let someone have a mistaken presumption, or let someone have a presumption that is not mistaken, but not in word, not in precision. If he knows the precision, he perishes himself, so that he may succeed in that intention by the better thing.

Furthermore, how does he call the perversion? To demonstrate that he is such a person, one who has turned aside; for example, many encounter the Scriptures and understand them as they ought not to. And no one else turned them aside except their own laziness. When someone therefore demonstrates such a person, that 'do not pay attention to him; he speaks errantly, what he says,' he has shown him to be turned aside, he has demonstrated him to be such. Do not become much righteous and do not philosophize excessively, lest you be struck with amazement. Do not be impiously much and do not become hard, so that you do not die not in your time (Job 20:5). And it has been said to us many times, that virtues are mediations, while their excesses and deficiencies are wickednesses. We say that wisdom...

ὀφείλει καταμένειν τῷ σοφίζεσθαι. "μὴ σοφίζου περισσά", μὴ ἐκγίνου τοῦ σοφὸς εἶναι καὶ ἐκπλαγῇς. μὴ ἀσεβήσῃς πολύ, μὴ γίνου σκληρός. 25 εἴπομεν, ὅτι ἔστιν τι γνωστὸν τοῦ θεοῦ, ᾧπερ ἐὰν ἐπῶμεν, ἀσεβοῦμεν. ἐκεῖνο δέ, ὃ ἐφανέρωσεν ἡμῖν ὁ θεός, ἐὰν γιγνώσκωμεν καὶ θέλωμ̣εν ἔχειν, οὐ βλαπτόμεθα. ἐὰν δὲ κἀκεῖνα τὰ μὴ ἐφικτὰ ἡμῖν θέλωμεν νοεῖν, ἐκπλητ τόμεθα καὶ ἀσεβοῦμεν πολύ. δυνατὸν δὲ καὶ τοῦτο λέγε̣ιν· εἴ ποτέ τι τῶν ἄλλων δυσχερὲς ἡμῖν καὶ δυςεύρετον φαίνεται̣, περὶ τούτου δὲ ἐπιχειρήσεις, οὐ βλάπτει· ἐπιχει ρητέον εἰς ἑκάτερα. ὅταν δὲ πε̣ρὶ θεοῦ ᾖν ὁ λόγος καὶ εἰς ἐκεῖνα χωρῇ ὁ θέλων εἰδέναι περὶ θεοῦ, ἃ μὴ δύναται, ἀσεβ̣εῖ πολὺ πέρα τοῦ δέοντος χωρῶν. οἷον πλῆθός εἰσιν οἱ ἄστερες. πᾶν δὲ πλῆθος ἢ περιττὸν ἢ ἄρτιόν ἐστιν. καὶ τὸ μὲν ἄρτιον εἰς δύο διαιρεῖται, τὸ δὲ περιττὸν ἔχει πλεο νάζον τὸ ἕτερον μέρος ἑνί. ἐὰν θέλωμεν περὶ τῶν ἀστέρων ἐπιχειρεῖν καὶ λέγειν, πρότερον περιττοὶ ἢ ἄρτιοι, οὐκ ἀσεβοῦμεν πολύ. ἔδει μὲν μὴ ἐπιχειρεῖν, περὶ ὧν οὐκ ἴσμεν. ὅμως οὐκ ἀσεβοῦμεν πολύ. ποιοῦμεν γὰρ τοῦτο, ὅτι ὁ οὐρανὸς κυκλοειδής ἐστιν καὶ εἰς δύο ἴσα τέμνεται ἡμισφαί ρια διαμέτρου ἀχθείσης εὐθείας. καὶ ἐπεὶ πάντοθεν ὁ οὐρανὸς ἠστέρωται, λέξει τις ὅτι ἴσων ὄντων τῶν ἡμικυκλίων ἐν ἑκάστῳ ἡμικυκλίῳ τοσοῦτοί εἰ σιν, ὅσοι καὶ ἐν τῷ λοιπῷ. καὶ κατασκευάζομεν ἐκ τούτου ἀρτίους αὐτοὺς εἶναι. καὶ οὐκ ἀσεβοῦμεν, κἄν τε οὕτως ἔχῃ κἂν μὴ ἔχῃ. γυμνασίας ἕνεκα ἡ ἐπιχείρησις γέγονεν. πάλιν ἐπειδὴ οἱ περὶ ἀριθμῶν πραγματευσάμενοι λέγουσιν τὸν περιττὸν ἰσχυρότερον εἶναι –δραστήριος γάρ ἐστιν– , ὁ δὲ ἄρτιος ὑλικώτερος– ὕλῃ γὰρ ἀνάκειται· ἡ δὲ ὕλη διαιρετή ἐστιν· πρώτη γὰρ
english: Folly has become a middle point between cunning and wickedness. Cunning is a surplus of wisdom. But cunning is praised in the Scripture, while among the Greeks it is reproached. And it is being reproached as cunning, and the Scripture calls it craftiness: 'O full of deceit and of all craftiness, son of the devil' (Acts 13:10). And even more, the New Testament reproaches cunning: 'For I fear lest, as the serpent deceived Eve in his cunning' (2 Corinthians 11:3); and also: 'But being a cunning man, I caught you by deceit' (1 Thessalonians 2:9). And still, concerning the heretics, he says that 'they walk in cunning, deceiving the word of the Lord' (2 Peter 3:16). Folly is a deficiency of wisdom.

And concerning all the virtues, this has been shown to us many times. We say, therefore, that piety exceeds reverence, but lacking it, [one is] the impious. And here, therefore, he intends to say: do not be too just; do not go outside of justice; seek to remain according to the standard, taking care of equality. Do not become too just; for many indeed have been accustomed to say: do not be strictly just, do not seek more than what is just. And it is possible also to take it this way, so that it may be most acceptable according to the will of Christianity. If it were to happen that you were wronged or that you should do wrong, do not be very just in giving what is just, since you do not do wrong. Desire rather to be wronged than to do wrong. Do not become, indeed, very just for the sake of not being wronged, but rather give yourself [over]. For in this way neither you will do wrong nor he, toward whom you have [the grievance].

And do not philosophize excessively, lest you be astonished. We say the same thing: do not philosophize beyond what is necessary, do not become outside of what is permitted to men. Such are those saying that we know God in the same way that He knows Himself. These philosophize excessively. Therefore also they are astonished, they become outside of their senses, they are found outside of logical observation. Do not philosophize excessively.

By logical reasoning, it is sometimes a discussion held for the sake of not letting the communion be broken, until I arrive at the right place and it is glorious and I am discussed with it. But if anyone thinks he succeeds in sophistry, he ought not to remain in sophistry. 'Do not sophistize excessively,' do not become too wise and be astonished. Do not be very impious, do not become hard.

We say that there is something known of God, which if we speak of, we are impious. But that which God has revealed to us, if we know it and wish to have it, we are not harmed. But if we also wish to intellectually grasp those things which are not attainable for us, we are astonished and we are very impious. And it is possible also to say this: if anything of the others seems difficult and hard to find for us, regarding this you should attempt to discuss; it does not harm; one should attempt regarding the separate things. But when the word is about God, and the one wishing to know about God reaches into those things which he is not able to, he is very impious by reaching beyond what is necessary.

For example, the stars are a multitude. And every multitude is either superfluous or exact. And the exact is divided into two, but the superfluous has one part having more than the other. If we wish to attempt and speak regarding the stars, first [saying] they are superfluous or exact, we are not very impious. It was necessary not to attempt regarding those things of which we do not know. However, we are not very impious. For we do this, because the heaven is circular and is cut into two equal hemispheres by a straight diameter being drawn. And since the heaven is starry everywhere, someone will say that the semicircles being equal, there are as many in each semicircle as in the rest. And from this we construct them to be exact. And we are not impious, whether it is so or not. The attempt has happened for the sake of exercise.
Again, since those having studied about numbers say that the superfluous is stronger—for it is active—and the exact is more material—for it consists of matter; and matter is divisible; for first...

english: The division in verse 217 occurs thus: for this reason they say that matter is a dyad—we were saying that it was necessary for the better of those seen by others to be subjected to the better number, and we construct from this that they are abundant. We do not act impiously in any way.

However, if someone says that we shall seek whether God is without beginning or not, the other part of the argument brings much impiety. Indeed, dialectic itself says that not all problems are dialectical. For those which are followed by punishment are not dialectical. For dialectical things aim at the two sides. No one wants to attempt whether God is or is not, or whether the laws should be kept beforehand or not; for these things have punishment following them in another form of the contradiction. For it brings shameful reputation to the one leading the other form of the contradiction.

And do not become hard. He who chooses evil becomes hard. For he constructs hardness for the one possessing it. 'For according to your hardness and your unrepentant heart, you are storing up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath' (Rom 2:5). You see that: having an unrepentant heart, one is found hard. And thus it happens to the heart of Pharaoh, which has been written of many times, having been hardened. 'Do not be excessively wise, do not become hard, so that you do not die in your time' (Prov 3:7).

This can be applied to everything; according to the intellect, it says: 'Do not become very hard; do not become, do not...' [text gapped]. It was found. It is good to hold fast to this, and not to let go of your hand from it. In each of the things said, you heard: do not become very righteous; hold fast to this. It has said, 'Do not be excessively wise.' In all the things said, hold fast as if in one genus.

Therefore, from what I have said, that it is also necessary to hold fast, do not let your practice [cease]. Persist in them, as the apostle says: 'Hold these things, be in these, so that your progress may become evident' (1 Tim 4:15), in the virtues. Meditating on these, it is necessary to remain in them, not to depart further from them. For it is not good to remain in other studies which are according to science and are conducted in an orderly fashion. And so that the demonstration may be from a ready example, the learning of letters of the first [elements]...

Let us take it. It is not good to remain in the study of characters, but to run quickly toward the next progress. Regarding virtues, practice brings progress: practice brings temperance, and one remains in temperance; practice brings justice, and one remains in justice; for in this way one is able to be shown to be diligent.

For he who fears God will come out of all things (Ps 112:7). Even if you have much help—help for coming out—it does not say that he becomes outside of all things. But 'to come out' signifies the end and the outcome, as we say that the holy voices that occurred regarding the coming of the Savior have attained an outcome. And this is 'so that it might be fulfilled' (Matt 2:17). For those from the heterodox, either maliciously or through ignorance, think that this fulfillment is to be taken in this way: that it might be fulfilled so that it might not be empty. And they say that the Old Testament was empty in itself and required fulfillment from without. Not this, but he speaks regarding an outcome: because of this Mary gave birth, 'so that it might be fulfilled; behold, she shall hold in her womb' (Luke 2:19). Because of this the Savior was crucified, because of 'they have pierced my hands and my feet' (Ps 22:16). He who fears God does not become outside of them, but reaches their end.

This is similar to what the apostolic text says: 'not of him who runs nor of him who wills, but of God who shows mercy' (Rom 9:16). Therefore, he who fears God 'comes out of all things' (Ps 112:7). For 'the fear of the Lord surpasses all things' (Ps 111:7). And if it surpasses all things, 'there is nothing above him.' For it is not the fear of punishment that is spoken of, but that one, about whom we say: 'there is no lack to those who fear him' (Ps 34:9). And 'He' is God. For He says: 'be holy to Him, for He is your fear' (Lev 19:2). Just as the one desiring wisdom becomes wisdom in Christ, and the righteousness of the righteous becomes righteousness in Christ, so also fear becomes so.

Wisdom will help the wise, while those exercising authority in the city are being overcome. Let us say that he who worships clings to all at once to those who are helping and to those who seem [to be so] to the many, being human things. For according to the true word, since all things are governed by the will of God, even things that seem to happen humanly are a gift from God. To have wealth is human, but 'the Lord makes rich' (1 Sam 2:7); to have the beginning is human, but the Lord 'establishes kings and deposes them' (1 Sam 2:7). english: As we are performing the work of providence, we say: some of these things are divine and god-befitting, while others are human.

Since he who says these things is most especially a king, he anoints all things toward piety; he says this because even if there are ten in authority in the city, and many are helping, and they surpass the opponents in number and power, if they do not have wisdom, they are not able to help the city.
Therefore, always seek the power of this general in his wisdom rather than in the multitude of his array.
"So then wisdom will help the wise one among the ten exercising authority in the city."
What is at hand to us has been given regarding history. If a city has many powerful men, but wisdom is lacking, they are not able to help the city.
And for the sake of an analogy, the world, the place around us, is called a city. If divine wisdom is not given, no one is able to pass through safely.
If wisdom does not help, those in authority can do nothing, even if they should be angels or holy men. If wisdom does not help, the city is not saved.

And each person's soul can also be called a city. If indeed someone has a myriad of human thoughts capable of helping this city, but divine wisdom does not help it and lead it and guard it toward the lawful, it is not able to be helped.

And observe "those who are in the city." You know that many times authority is taken from without. And you have in the histories of the Scriptures that many times those who were [acting] against Israel and its kings hired other kings.
But the ones hired from without do not contribute to helping the city as the natives do. Indeed, when they see that the matter is weak, they withdraw and are favorable toward the opponents.

"Therefore, those who are in the city"; even if they are rich and are well-disposed toward it and are even well-prepared for this very thing, to help the city, in the absence of wisdom they are not able to endure what is urgent.

For man is not righteous in the land (Ecclesiastes 7:20). He did not say at once that a man is not righteous, but in the land. And as is at hand, I am not speaking regarding history, but regarding moral instruction as regarding a way of speaking; I say this, that those...

The man on earth is the one 'walking according to the flesh' (Rom 8:4), according to 'you indeed die as men' (1 Cor 15:3). This one is on earth not only in body, but also in heart. He 'sets his mind on earthly things' (Col 3:2), and 'sinks himself into his seat'. No one of such people is righteous.

I say 'man' not simply, but the one not being on earth who is able to be righteous. 'If one walks on earth, having his portion in heaven', he is wise not on earth. Because of this, the one having righteousness is not prevented from being called a lawbreaker from it. Furthermore, why do you not stand according to history? If you wish to take it according to history, you descend into a dogma, that there is no man born on earth without sin.

I said, that this brings us labor regarding John and regarding this Jeremiah, unless indeed you take that sin, according to which it has been said: 'all have sinned' (Rom 3:23). You know, however, that I once omitted this and said that not every sin brings harm to the one doing it, when I also use an icon such as this, that a painter is learning the art: many icons are drawn not well, and this sin bringing [them] is not a mockery. Because of this, he draws not well, so that he may learn to draw well. And many things must be done sinfully, so that someone might thus correctly achieve the goal of his work.

They also say concerning the inventors, that the inventors were not such as those who had existed before them when they were practicing. The painters are called indeed 'old', because they drew so much deviated from the original forms, so that the icon might happen to be less than the writing. Thus, therefore, you would say that everyone becoming on earth has this sin, not the one opposing virtue, but the one bringing [it] upon virtue.

Indeed, regarding the one striving to draw an icon, having begun the art, we sometimes say of the one drawing badly that the one already seasoned in the art draws better, if that one draws carelessly out of laziness; and if you compare the work to the work, the one of the careless is better; but if you look toward the intention, he who wrote by hand wrote more. Thus, therefore, we take [it] by analogy of quantity. The one able to learn in ten years, having learned, we say [he has learned] twelve; we have learned much.

source_text: τὸν δὲ δυ 221 νάμενον πεντήκοντα, ἐκμαθόντα δὲ τετταράκοντα λέγομεν μηδὲν ἐκμεμαθη κέναι. ὃς ποιήσει ἀγαθὸν καὶ οὐχ ἁμαρτήσεται. ὁ τοιοῦτος οὐκ ἔστιν ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς ἄνθρωπος, ὃς ποιήσει ἀγαθὸν καὶ οὐχ ἁμαρτήσεται. ὑψηλοτέραν θέλω λαβει῀̣ν δ̣ιάνοιαν· ἀλλὰ μή μοι ἀπει ροκαλίαν ἐπιγράψητε. περὶ μόνου τοῦ Ἰησοῦ εἴρηται· "πρὶν π̣ροέληται πο νηρά, ἐκλέξεται τὸ ἀγαθόν." μόνον το`̣ π̣αιδίον τὸ κατὰ τὸν Ἰησοῦν, τὸ "μὴ ἐγνωκότα ἁμαρτίαν", προαίρεσιν τῶν πονηρῶν, εἵλατο τὸ ἀγαθο´̣ν, πάντες δὲ οἱ ἄλλοι μετὰ τὸ γνῶναι πονηρίαν ταύτην τὴν τιμωμένην, οὐ τὴν ἐπίψογον, ἀλλ̣ὰ τὴν εἰσαγομένην. "πρὶν προελέσθαι πο̣ν̣η̣ρά"· ἁμαρ τεῖν οὔπ̣οτ̣' η᾿̣δυ´̣νατο, ὅτι μέχρι προπαθείας γινόμενος οὐκ ἐκτείνε̣ι ταύ την εἰς δ̣ι̣άθεσιν. δύναται οὖν εἰς τὸ αὐτὸ ἄγεσθαι, δύναται δὲ καὶ ἑτέρως νοεῖσθαι, ὅτι ἐν τῷ ναῷ τῷ ἀνθρώπῳ γέγονεν ὁ θεὸς Λόγος. ὁ θεὸς δὲ Λόγος 28 καὶ σοφία ἐστίν, καὶ ἐκ ταύτης τῆς διανοίας πᾶσα βελτίωσίς ἐστιν. ἐπει δὴ δὲ τὰ τῆς οἰκονομίας λέγω, τοῦτο̣ ὧδ̣ε̣ ὀφείλει δειχθῆναι. παιδίον ὂν οὐκ ἐκεῖνα ἔλεγεν, ἃ εἶπεν α᾿̣νὴρ τέλειος γεν̣άμενος. προέκοπτεν οὖν τὴν προκοπήν. οὕτω λημπτέον· διδάσκαλος ἢ ἄλλος ὁμοι´̣ως ἔχων τὴν 222 τῆς παιδεύσεως ἕξιν προσεληλυθότων μαθη̣τῶν καὶ ἐφιεμένων τῆς ἐπιστήμης σ̣υνκαταβαίνει καὶ ἐκεῖνα λέγει, ἃ δύνανται οἱ εἰςαγόμενοι ἀκοῦσαι, οὐχ ἃ αὐτὸς δύναται, καὶ συνσχηματίζεται τῇ ἀγνοίᾳ τῶν εἰσαγομένων, καὶ ὡς αὐτὰ μόνα εἰδὼς ἃ λέγει παιδεύει αὐτούς. ὅσον οὖν πρ̣οκόπτει τὸ παιδίον, προκόπτει καὶ ὁ διδάσκαλος· ἀλλὰ τὸ μὲν παιδίον προκόπτει προσλήμψει μαθημάτων, ὁ δὲ διδάσκαλος προκόπτει ἀναδείξε̣ι̣ τῆς ἐν ούσης δυνάμεως. καὶ λαβέ μοι τὸν ἥλιον φθάσαντα ε᾿̣πὶ τ̣ὸν ὁρίζοντα τοῦτον τὸν αἰσθητόν· ὑποτρέχον δέ τι κάλυμμα κωλυέτω τὴν ὄψιν ταχέως ἐπιβα λεῖν, ὡς εἰ μὴ ἦν τὸ κάλυμμα. ὅσον γ̣ίνετ̣αι περὶ τὴν ὄψιν φανέρωσις, τότε καὶ τοῦ ἡλίου γίνεται τοσαύτη. κ̣αὶ λέγω προκόπτειν τὸν ἥλιον, οὐ προσλήμψει φωτός, ἀλλὰ τῷ δύνασθαι λοιπὸν φωτίσαι τὸν πρότερον οὐ δυ νάμενον οὕτως καταλάμπεσθαι. κάλυμμα οὖν ψυχῆς ἐστιν ἡ ἁμαρτία. ἐὰν οὖν μὴ ἐκλέγῃ τὴν κακίαν, τὸ φῶς φανερώτερον ἑαυτὸ δείκνυσιν. ουτως οὕτως οὖν λέγω τὸν διδάσκαλον προκόπτειν σοφίᾳ, οὐ προσλήμψει σοφίας, ἀλλὰ ἀναδείξει πλείονος σο φίας. ἐπὶ τῷ ὄντι καὶ προκοπὴ πᾶσα ἐνεπο̣δ̣ίζετ̣ο, εἰ μή, φέρε, ἄρτιοι ἅγιοι ὁρατοὶ ὄντες τοσαῦτα ἠδύναντο ἐνεργ̣ε̣ῖν καὶ ἐγνωκέναι. εἰ ἄνδρες γε νόμενοι πεποίηκαν καὶ εἰρήκασιν μεγαλά, ἔστι τοῦτ̣ο̣ εἰς προκοπὴν ἀρε τῆς καὶ ἀνάδειξιν. english: Regarding the one called fifty, having learned forty, we say that nothing has been learned out. He who will do good and will not sin—such a man does not exist on the earth. I desire to attain a higher intellect; but do not write an unasked-for reproach upon me. Concerning Jesus alone it has been said: 'Before evil things come, he chooses the good' (Matt 20:16). Only the Child, according to Jesus, who 'did not know sin' (Luke 2:52), by the choice of the evil ones, chose the good; but all the others, after knowing this evil—the kind that is punished, not the kind that is merely falling into it, [failed]. 'Therefore there is no man who will do good and will not sin.' All possess the good along with sin, but sin is that which has been spoken of, that which exists prior to virtue.

Behold, many, thinking they have an alertness of intellect and having surrendered to their own alertness, imagine they know all things; and when they begin to rise up regarding those things they think they know, they fall into such ignorance as to say they have unlearned the learning. And we know by experience: many times I have reasoned about a certain thing, thinking it was easy to understand, and it appeared more difficult to all those with individual intellects. This ignorance is before knowledge; and it is not contrary to knowledge, but before knowledge. He who thus thinks he knows, if he does not find himself as one who knows nothing, he is unable to receive knowledge.

Therefore, there is only one, concerning whom this has been said: 'Before evil things come, he chose the good' (Matt 20:16). Even if it does not seem so to Apollinarius and those with him, their doctrine is refuted. 'Before evil things come to pass'; he was never able to sin, because until he became subject to passion, he did not extend this into a disposition. He is able, therefore, to be led to the same [state], but it can also be understood otherwise: that in the human temple, the God Logos has come to be. And the God Logos is wisdom, and from this intellect all improvement is. Since, then, I am speaking of the things of the economy, this ought to be shown here. Being a child, he did not say those things which he would have said having become a perfect man. He was therefore progressing in advancement. Thus it should be taken: a teacher, or another similarly having the nature of instruction.

When six disciples have come and are filled with knowledge, he descends with them and says those things which those being led in are able to hear, not what he himself is able to [say], and it is shaped according to the ignorance of those being led, and as if he instructs them knowing only those things. Just as much as the child progresses, so the teacher progresses; but while the child progresses by the reception of lessons, the teacher progresses by the manifestation of the power that is present.

Take for me the sun having descended upon this sensible horizon; but run and get a covering to quickly obstruct the sight, as if the covering were not there. Just as much as a revelation becomes regarding sight, so much also happens of the sun. And I say the sun progresses, not by the reception of light, but by the ability to illuminate the remainder, which previously was not able to shine in this way. Sin, therefore, is a covering of the soul. If, therefore, one does not cast off wickedness, the light shows itself more clearly to itself. Thus, therefore, I say the teacher progresses in wisdom, not by the reception of wisdom, but by the manifestation of greater wisdom.

In reality, every progress was hindered, unless—come now—the worthy saints, being visible, were able to work and to know so many things. If indeed men, being known, have done and have spoken great things, this is for the progress of virtue and its manifestation. And indeed, regarding all words which they will speak, do not give your heart, so that you may not hear your slave as he is rebuking you, because many times he will act wickedly. And indeed, regarding many words which men will speak, there is a certain ignorance and sin; ... of those beginning the discoveries of the learned.

And saying, 'do not give your heart,' he passes into a moral lesson. You know that the ... sins and iniquities occurring against someone, provoke him to indignation. If therefore you command, and the slaves are easy-tempered toward those commanding, do not 'give your heart' to this, because you also will be harmed there. If, therefore, a slave curses you, observe him: whether he does what was commanded or does not do it, not how he does it or does not do it. For later you want to know this, so that you may honor freedom, so that you may give to him that which he did not have before. Observe.

source_text: οὖν καὶ σὺ σεαυτόν, εἰ οὐχ ἥμαρτές πο τε. τοῦτο γὰρ καὶ ὁ ἀπόστολος γράφει προτρεψάμενος τοὺς δούλους ὑπο κεῖσθαι τοῖς δεσπόταις "μὴ κατ' ὀφθαλμοδουλίαν", "ἀλλ' ὡς Χριστοῦ δούλους". λέγει· "καὶ ὑμεῖς οἱ δεσπόται τὴν ἰσότητα πρὸς τοὺς δούλους ἔχετε." ὁ ἔχων τὴν ἰσότητα πρὸς τοὺς δούλους οὐκ ἐπίκειται καὶ τὰς διαθέσεις αὐτῶν σκοπεῖ, ἀλλὰ τὸ ἔργον, τί γέγονεν· καὶ οὐκ ἀκαί ρως χρησόμεθα. φέρομεν οὖν ἔν τισιν εὐαγγελίοις· γυνή, φησίν, κατεκρίθη ὑπὸ τῶν Ἰουδαίων ἐπὶ ἁμαρτίᾳ καὶ ἀπεστέλλετο λιθοβοληθῆναι εἰς τὸν τόπον, ὅπου εἰώθει γίνεσθαι. ὁ σωτήρ, φησίν, ἑωρακὼς αὐτὴν καὶ θεωρήσας ὅτι ἕτοιμοί εἰσιν πρὸς τὸ λιθ̣οβολη῀̣σαι αὐτήν, τοῖς μέλλουσιν αὐτὴν κατα βαλεῖν λίθοις εἶπεν· "ὃς οὐχ ἥμαρτεν, αἰρέτω λίθον καὶ βαλέτω εαὐ τόν." εἴ τις σύνοιδεν ἑαυτῷ τὸ μὴ ἡμαρτηκέναι, λαβὼν λίθον παισάτω αὐ τήν. καὶ οὐδεὶς ἐτόλμησεν· ἐπιστήσαντες ἑαυτοῖς καὶ γνόντες, ὅτι καὶ αὐτοὶ ὑπεύθυνοί εἰσίν τισιν, οὐκ ἐτόλμησαν καταπταῖσαι ἐκείνην. ὅτι πλειστάκις πονηρεύσεται. "πλειστάκις πονηρεύσεται" τοῦ κακῶσαι. ἀλλὰ μὴ σκόπει σὺ τοῦ το. μέχρι βουλῆς αὐτῷ ἵσταται τὸ πρᾶγμα. εἰ δέ π̣οτ̣ε τ̣ῷ ὀ´̣ν̣τ̣ι̣ τ̣ο̣ι̣ο̣υ῀̣τ̣ο´̣ τι φανείη ὡς ἀληθῶς τολμήσαντος αὐτοῦ, τότε κωλυτέον αὐτόν, τότε ἐπιστατέον, οἷς λέγει βουλήμασιν α̣ὐτ̣ο̣υ῀̣. καὶ καθόδους πολλὰς κακώσει καρδίαν σου, ὅτι ὡς καί γε σὺ κατηράσω ἑτέρους. "καθόδους πολλὰς" λέγει, ἃς ἔρχεται πολλάκις. ὁ δὲ πολλάκις ····· ····· ····τι ου᾿̣κ ἐνεργεῖ. καὶ ὅταν λέγω περί τινος, ὅτι· πολλάκις τυ····· ····· · σημαίνω, ὅτι οὐκ ἔτυψα. μέχρι τοῦ καρδίαν σου κακηγο ρῆσαι ····· ·. ὅτι ὡς καί γε σὺ κατηράσω 29 ἑτέρους. "πάντα ὅσα θέλετε, ἵνα ποιῶσιν ὑμῖν οἱ ἄνθρωποι, καὶ αὐτοῖς ποι̣ε̣ῖ τε." "ὃ μισεῖς, ἑτέρῳ οὐ μὴ ποίει." ὡς ἐμίσεις, ὅτε πολλάκις κατηρῶ, κα̣ι`̣ α̣ὐτ̣ὸς καταρᾶσθαι μίσει. καὶ τὸ τὸν δοῦλον ποιῆσαι γνωσθῆναι καὶ ἐν τούτῳ πο̣λλ̣····· ········ λαβε ἀπαίτει· ἐκ σεαυτοῦ τὴν συν χώρησιν λαβέ. πάντα ταῦτα ἐπείρασα ἐν τῇ σοφίᾳ· εἶπα· σοφισθήσομαι, καὶ αὐτὴ ἐμ̣ακρύνθη ἀπ' ἐμοῦ μακρὰν ὑπὲρ ὃ ἦν. ἐν τῇ σοφίᾳ τῇ δοθείσῃ μοι θεοπ̣έμπτῳ οὔσῃ ταῦτα̣ ἐπείρασα ἐγώ, ὁ ἐκκλησιάζων, ἐγώ, ὁ σοφός, ὁ παιδευτὴς̣ τῶν ε᾿̣π̣ι̣σ̣τ̣η̣μῶν, ὁ οὕτως προ̣ 224 άγων τοὺς λόγους̣, ὡς λυσιτελεῖ τοῖς μανθάνουσιν. ἵνα τὸν πειρασμὸν λάβωμεν, ὡς λέγουσιν αὐτὸν οἱ φρόνιμοι, πειραστι κὴ ἐπιχείρησις καὶ συλλογισμὸς πειραστικός ἐστιν οὗτος, ὅταν ἐκ τῶν δοξῶν τοῦ προσδιαλεγομένου λαμβάνωμεν τὰς προτάσ̣εις. οἷον ἐὰν λέγωμεν, εἰ ἀγαθὸς ὁ πλοῦτος ἢ οὐκ ἀγαθός, ουκ ἐκ τῶν δοξῶν τούτο̣υ̣, πρὸς ὃν ἔχο μεν τὸν λόγον, τὰς προτάσεις λαμβάνομεν, ἀλλ' οὐκ ἐκ τοῦ καθόλου. καὶ λέγομεν, ὅτι ἔστιν τῷ πλούτῳ δεόντως χρήσασθαι. ἔστιν τοὺς πλησίον εὐεργετῆσαι, ἄνδρας σοφοὺς θρέψαι, οὓς εἶπεν ὁ ἀπόστολος· "ταῖς χρεί αις τῶν ἁγίων κοινωνοῦντες." καὶ ἐκ τούτου κατεσκευάζομεν, ὅτι ἔστιν ἀγαθῶς τ̣ῷ πλούτῳ χρήσασθαι. ὁ ἕτερος ὁ λέγων, ὅτι οὐκ ἀγαθός, λέγει· πολλοὶ ἐκ πλούτου ἄσωτοι γεγένηνται, μοιχοὶ ὤφθησαν, καὶ ὅτι μέθαις σχολάζει ὁ πλούσιος, ὅτι ἐπιβουλεύσεται πολλάκις. ἐκ τῶν δοξῶν γὰρ τοῦ ἀποκρινομένου ποιούμεθα τὰς ἐπιχειρήσεις, κἂν μὴ ἄλλοι οὕτω δοξάζωσιν, ἀλλὰ αὐτὸς μόνος. καὶ λέγεται οὗτος ὁ συλλογισμὸς πειραστι κός· πείρας γὰρ ἕνεκα ἐπάγεται. καὶ ὁμοίως ἔχει τῷ λεγομένῳ παρὰ τοῖς γεωμέτραις ψευδογραφήματι· τοῖς μανθα´̣ν̣ουσιν καὶ δυναμένοις ἢ δηλοῖ ποτε̣ γν̣ωσ̣θῆν̣αι ·····ε̣ε̣ι̣σ̣ον̣ ····β̣εσθ···· ἐπιστήμης ἢ οὔ. ποιεῖ ψευδογράφημα ὁ γεωμέτρης καὶ ····· ····· ···· δ̣υ´̣ο̣ ψεύδη καὶ δίδωσιν ἐκείνῳ λῦσαι. ἐὰν ἐν τῇ λύσει ····· ····· ···· ε̣ὑ῀̣ρεν ἐτ̣εὰ κ̣αὶ πεῖραν ἔδειξεν τελειότητος. ἔστιν οὗτος ····· ····· ···ε γὰρ τιθεὶς λήμματα μεταξὺ τῶν λημμάτων ε᾿̣κ̣ε̣ι῀̣να τίθησιν ····· ····· ····
english: Therefore so also you, if you have not sinned at all. For this also the apostle writes, exhorting the slaves to lie under the masters, not by eye-service, but as slaves of Christ. He says: 'And you masters, have equality toward the slaves' (Col 4:1). The one having equality toward the slaves does not look upon and scrutinize their dispositions, but the work, what has become, and we shall not use them unsuitably.

We bring therefore in some gospels: a woman, he says, was judged by the Jews on account of sin and was being sent to be stoned in the place where it was customary to happen. The Savior, he says, having seen her and having perceived that they were ready to stone her, said to those about to cast stones at her: 'He who has not sinned, let him take a stone and cast it at herself' (John 8:7). If anyone understood to himself that he had not sinned, having taken a stone, let him strike her. And no one dared; having realized for themselves and knowing that they also are responsible in some way, they did not dare to strike her.

Because many times it will do evil. 'Many times it will do evil' to harm. But do not look at that, until the matter stands by his will. And if ever to the existing thing of that kind something should appear as him truly daring, then it is to be prevented, then it is to be supervised, by the intentions which he has. And many descents will harm your heart, because just as you also cursed others. 'Many descents' he says, which come many times. And the 'many times' ... what it does not work. And when I say concerning someone, that: many times you... I signify that I did not fail. Until to speak evil to your heart... because just as you also cursed others. 'All that you want, so that men may do to you, and also do to them' (Matt 7:12). 'What you hate, you will not do to another.' As you will hate, when many times you curse, he himself will be hated to be cursed. And to do to the slave to be known...

In this, many things are taken away; take from yourself the capacity for endurance. I attempted all these things in wisdom; I said, 'I will become a sophist,' and it itself moved far away from me, further than it was.

In the wisdom given to me, being God-sent, I attempted these things—I, the one preaching, I, the wise, the instructor of the sciences, the one who thus drives the arguments so that they are effective to those learning. In order that we may take the test, as the prudent say, a testing attempt and a testing syllogism is this, when we take the propositions from the opinions of the one being argued with. For example, if we say whether wealth is good or not good, we do not take the propositions from the opinions of this person to whom I have the argument, but not from the general. And we say that it is necessary to use wealth properly: to do good to neighbors, to support wise men, whom the apostle said, 'participating in the needs of the saints' (Hebrews 13:16). And from this we construct that it is good to use wealth properly.

The other, saying that it is not good, says: many have become lawless from wealth, adulterers were seen, and that the rich man idles with drinking, and that he will often plot greedily. For from the opinions of the one responding we make our attempts, even if others do not so suppose, but he alone. And this syllogism is called testing; for it is brought forward for the sake of a test. And it is similar to what is said by the geometers regarding a false figure: to those learning and capable of sometimes making evident whether a science exists or not. The geometer makes a false figure and two falsehoods and gives them to that person to solve. If in the solution he found the truth and showed a proof of perfection. For he is this, because having placed certain premises between the premises, he places them there...

english: I said: I shall become wise. The 'I said' here signifies not only the vocalizing, but the disposition of being in such a state as 'no one says: Lord, Lord, unless he be in the Holy Spirit' (Matt 7:21). To say here is to truly confess, to truly say that he serves Him as Lord. And here 'I said': I added this to become wise. The fully spoken example becomes clear; in this, as much as we thought we had wisdom, we did not say: 'I shall become wise.' But now, instead of saying: 'I lack wisdom,' I say: 'I shall become wise; but it has become far from me, beyond what it was.'

We thought it was not at all near to be mine, and for this reason I strove to do all things to receive it now. And when I have done this, it has become far from me. But in reality it has not become far from me, rather to me it appeared to become far, exceeding the distance, a deep depth; who will find it? Instead of: 'one is not finding it.'

Furthermore, you do not say of an ascent: 'do not give your heart' (Deut 6:5); it is indeed ethical. One must take this: the body is a slave of the soul. Therefore, this says: 'do not give your heart' to be controlled by the evil impulses of the body. Let us say, if it ever controls, that the body is able to rise up against the soul through desires, through passions. Do not, therefore, understand this in such a way as to know what he says or what he was saying. His starting point must be examined. This word harms; it is a curse. And if the word is a curse, it is a prayer for evils.

'He who subdues the body and enslaves it' does not allow it to know his heart through investigation. I and my heart have encircled the goal to know and to contemplate and to seek wisdom and judgment. The heart has often already been said to signify the mind. But the mind does not deviate, nor does it fit into a straight line, but it turns around itself. Indeed, even some of those from the outside have said that thoughts are like wheels and turning circles. For when the mind reaches out toward external things and wishes to receive the imagination of the sensible things, it is not about itself, it does not turn about itself. But when it thinks and stands upon itself, it is both the thinking and the thing being thought. For the mind in its activity is always the act of thinking.

It has [this property], and it is not [the case] when it lies upon the external things. What about 'I and my heart'? Each of the many things lying together or being thought of is called the whole. Man consists of soul and body and spirit, as if he says, 'your whole spirit and soul and body,' not saying all other things of the man. But each is a different thing of him, yet the man is all at once.

The apostle has done this also regarding the body, even if he mentioned something intelligible: 'if the whole is an eye, and if the whole is an ear, where is the body?' (Matt 5:29) and he says that each member is by itself, but all together the body. And it is seen in a similar way. The name of the 'vote' here signifies the number. The meanings are many; the many things divide a greatest theory. And one might say 'vote' as if it were a number.

But if someone wishes to take the 'vote' as the thing said: 'and when they were being removed, he brought a vote' (Acts 5:28), the testimony, and thus he desired 'to know wisdom and a vote.' If wisdom is the knowledge of divine and human things and the causes of these, each ought to perceive, and thus the whole knowledge is already decided. And to know the impiety, folly, and confusion of the impious. It is a great thing to know the inferior things, not necessarily to perform them. It is impossible to turn away from evil without having thought it.

On the other hand, we say 'not knowing sin' of the one not sinning, instead of 'he has no experience of sin.' Thus Jesus did not 'know sin,' that is, he was not tested. But he who intends to abstain from evil will know it, because it is bad and because it will bring evil to the one acting, and because 'it brings down unto death' (Prov 5:5) and because it is elective and can be released by us. It does not exist by essence, nor is it produced by the movement of the stars. If, therefore, he knows this folly of the fool, I stand away from it, casting it out. And to know through the impious the joy. This says: if I know who the impious is, and I abstain from him, I know the joy. For the 'because of what' must be heard thus: 'for through law is the knowledge of sin' (Rom 3:20). He who knows the law through it enters into sin, clearly, and also virtue; but the one [knows] in order to do, the other in order to flee. And confusion and wandering.

english: Folly, impiety, and coarseness are [these things]. For even the external sophist-lover has spoken of sophistic disturbances. And it is necessary to know a turning about, that these things must be turned around, not held permanently. Even if they sometimes stand in the soul, it is not necessary to have them, but to turn them around and turn away from them.

And I find her more bitter than death along with the woman, who is a beast. I find her, the coarseness that turns around, 'more bitter than death'—because when I take experience of her, I die; I consider her more bitter than death. But if someone considers her death and the destruction of the soul, he will reject her, he will cease from her. Along with the woman, who is a beast. It is possible also to say this opinion, which is the most skillful, that she is a woman whom he rejects, whom he saw bringing nothing other than death.

For the opinions and the habit of the women say much regarding the praiseworthy and the scurrilous, as if saying: 'Does Wisdom not bring prudence to a man?' and 'Your wife is like a fruitful vine, your sons like young olive shoots.' From this woman, male offspring are produced, nourished by fire and light. For the blessing of these kinds is that fire and light nourish them.

But again it is said scurrilously: 'Do not pay attention to a bad woman,' it says, 'the lips of a prostitute withdraw, which for a little while sweetens the pharynx. Later, however, you will find [her] more bitter than bile.' Then after a little while it brings [this]: 'the feet of folly'; he said the woman is folly. Therefore also he distributed her before wisdom.

He says that this woman, whom he said is a turning about, whom he had as coarseness, is a beast, not a hunted thing. It is possible also to say this, that someone measures the evil, not as a certain day, but as a wild beast springing upon himself. And it is possible, for the sake of the spoken moral instruction, to take the bad woman to be signified according to the bad history. You know that sins happen to be appropriate to certain [things]. Mostly, to carry [it] is a man's thing to wander about sophistically, but for a woman it is to be brought forward in incontinence. Therefore he says this woman, whom he calls a prostitute, whom he calls 'sitting on a couch' and 'calling to those passing by,' is a beast.

It is a snare, even if you take it as a disposition: the cunning and malicious disposition, and the sophistical or heretical one; she is a bad woman. And her heart is a fishhook, and bonds are in her hands; the good will be set apart from her before God, and the sinner will be caught in her. She wants to fish for those approaching. And contrary to this is the fishhook which Jesus cast into the sea. For the net of the divine discipline and of the evangelical teaching is 'a snare cast into the sea and draws from every kind' (Matt 13:47). And since the snare is not perceptible, neither are the things being fished for perceptible. If, therefore, it says, 'from every kind,' it says this: 'from every kind of human character that has fallen into the watery life.'

And concerning the devil it is said in one of the twelve prophets—and this is Amos—'Will he be silent in swallowing up the ungodly the righteous? And will you make men like the fish of the sea and like the creeping things that have no leader?' (Amos 4:2). For he says: 'He drew to a conclusion in a hook and gathered in his net. Because of this, he sacrifices to his net and offers sacrifice to his bob. His bob always wavers, and will he show no mercy in killing nations?' Thus the enemy hunts differently, just as 'the Word of salvation' does. For Jesus 'cast [it] into the sea' as a snare, and 'Peter is about to cast [nets].' And some teachings are such that, looking at each one, they say specifically what kind of [person] it is. For when it gathers diverse nations by a snare, it is: 'it will show no mercy in killing nations.'

And since the predecessors of false doctrines make them as if they were a divine art or offer sacrifice to them as to a god. This woman, therefore, having been called to have snares, has in her own heart because of her many-sided way of hereticalizing and seizing men, the snare is of the devil. Here we wish to understand that of Job, so that from him and from this we may take the theory. He says that 'no swimming thing coming together will let even one scale of its tail, nor shall the ships of fishermen [touch] its head' (Job 41:1). Then he says: 'Who will uncover its face? And for the folding of its skin, who would enter?' (Job 41:11). No one is able to uncover its face. Multi-

english: He is a person, imitating the deceptive Protagonist; for he does not have a face that is entirely ordered. Thus he says in Job: 'Who will strip off his face-covering?' (Job 13:23). You cannot say that this is his face. If you lift his face by word or by thought, something worse is found. Furthermore, he is folded up everywhere; 'into the folding of his armor' no one can enter. And if you enter, it is folded up again.

So also here the wicked woman called here—whether you mean regarding rhetoric or regarding opinion—does not have one snare. When you think you have escaped one, she lays another. A bond is in her hands. She immediately binds the one approaching. Her hand refers to practice and energy. The one acting according to her is not only hunted and snared, but also falls into a bond; he is judged a prisoner. The good man will be taken out from her before the face of God. The good man before the face of God is not such in essence, but the one hurrying to have virtue, so that he may become even more good for God. This one, therefore, does not fall into her, is not hunted, is not snared. But the foolish one is handed over to the good man 'not falling into her snares' or into the bonds. And 'being handed over' is often interpreted: after many times preventing, when that evil no longer prevents, a handing over to him occurs. And he will be caught sinning in her. No one sinless is caught by her. The beginning of being caught is having sinned. Indeed, it approaches even the saints; but since they do not sin, they are not caught by her, but are outside her, trampling her.

Furthermore: the ascent. Did I encircle [it] to know? It is a whole ascent; we say this. It is not far from what was said, that, since 'the maker of them is seen through the greatness of beauty and of creatures' (Wisdom 13:5), the one circling the whole cosmos and seeing all that God made, sees them as 'very beautiful' (Gen 1:31). But if he does not circle, but takes one by one, he does not see the beauty of the created. So, therefore, if one does not circle all the doctrines and all the virtues and their sequence, and all the creation and through it...
By knowing the creation, one knows the Creator, according to His power. Then, having grasped all things together in thought as if circling, wisdom finds the truth.

'Behold, I have found this,' says the Preacher (Eccl 5:7), 'one single thought to find, which my soul sought and did not find.' The Preacher is the teacher of the general assembly. 'The Preacher found this'—the 'finding' here is 'grasping.' But what kind? This very thing: that the woman who exists has snares in her heart and a bond in her own hand. To know this is of the Preacher. For this will benefit those listening to the Preacher.

Regarding 'one single'—since he speaks here in the plural; for it is not spoken about only one alone, that 'one single.' We mean, that is, about her snares; he says that her deceits and her snares find a foolish thought and teach it. For indeed, these women also mislead one another and lead forward not toward finding a good thought, but toward being cunning. But did he not say 'one' above? The evil is not single, but rather many and widely spread.

Listen closely, for he does not say these things about a specific woman, but about every woman having such zeal, 'one single thought to find.' And if you take it regarding the snares, you say that even the snares seem to be in agreement. For those professing false doctrines attempt to say that their false opinions agree. 'Which my soul sought and did not find.' My soul sought their thought, and did not find it. It is difficult to hunt. It is like the things said: 'Do we not ignore His thoughts?' (Job 11:6) 'Who could enter to strike His armor?' (Job 11:4).

But what then is the 'found' in the preceding? Here he says additionally: 'one single thought to find.' This thought I desired to see, so that I might also teach them. And 'did not find' can be said in such a way as 'not of the one willing nor the one running, but of the God who shows mercy.' From myself I found nothing. But God revealed to me; He showed me the cunning of this thought. For he does not say that the one running and the one willing achieves nothing.

english: He found one man out of a thousand, and a woman he found not in all these things. Many manuscripts have 'a man'; 'but a woman in all these things he found not.' If you can take it literally, that a diligent man barely finds one man out of a thousand, but a diligent woman is not to be found in all these. Or thus: he found a man, one of the thousand, a single thought of a man from many, but a woman not, because of her being hard to hunt, because of her being hard to grasp—is he saying he has found this? For it is a prey.

It is one thing to know someone as a sophist, and another to grasp his sophisms. For he who guards himself from falling into sophisms knew that he has a sophist against him, but he is not always able to untie his sophisms. But to find truly is that is, to see his craft, to make his deception manifest. Furthermore, see, he found this, which God made with the upright man, and they themselves sought many thoughts. The essence of this observation is this: God made man upright, that is, good and well, having nothing crooked or bent. But they themselves found many thoughts.

According to those thoughts, these are the differences: that 'he is a certain prey', that 'to find one thought with the one', that 'someone is a fool'. They were saying that the enemy is complex, when I mentioned the First. But he certainly has a face resembling himself, in that he is Satan, in that he is the Accuser. This face of his only those are able to see who say, 'for we do not ignore his thoughts.' They know what kind of a deceptive face he has, being imposed from without, and what kind of a face is, as if according to his nature, his face. But according to his nature, his face is that which sinks into evil. And you find often sophist men having ten thousand faces around them, and they have one hidden aim.

Therefore, that is his face. Just as he moves from these to those who are praised, there is a certain face of the man, according to which he is a man, not according to which he is an evil man or a cunning man.

This is the one who has become in honor: 'a man being in honor does not fail' (Prov 22:4), as the man having become 'both in image and in likeness' (Gen 1:26) of God. And this indeed is his preceding face, which if anyone should look upon and contemplate, he would find the man.

But they did not achieve one single calculation, but many. For wickedness is manifold. And I have once spoken aloud an image regarding the process of division, that all those who succeed find the same number, but those who err do not find the same.

A man therefore has a face, according to which he is rational, according to which he does all things with reason; and just as I was saying regarding the judge: the true judge is a living soul, just. He observes nothing other than the facts of the things being judged, not whether they are friends or enemies or relatives. For the good of the judgment depends on this.

And observe that he did not say 'property was cast away,' but 'to the properties.' And there is one form of man which makes him like God, but there are many, into which he falls. When he becomes cunning, he bears the face of a fox. When harmful and injurious, [he bears the face of] a serpent; when wild, a lion; when uncontrolled and a lover of pleasure and a flatterer, a dog. And entirely from the one man and the one form, variety and manifoldness arise.

And again the purpose will be, even if it seems not to some, by which the rejection of all forms occurs, to bear [them] so that that which God has made might be revealed. When, therefore, he remained in identity, he had one calculation. And just as it is said in one of the Psalms: 'God dwells with the single-minded in his house' (Ps 11:3), those dwelling piety, uprightly, and ecclesiastically are single-minded, 'being equipped with the same mind and the same purpose,' as each is to be single-minded.
